pos: v.t. (to lower in value, dignity, or purity; to degrade)
etymology: From de-, down, + base, from Latin bassus, low; to bring a thing down from its proper worth or standing.
biblical_def:
And thou wentest to the king with ointment, and didst increase thy perfumes, and didst send thy messengers far off, and didst debase thyself even unto hell.

Isaiah is indicting Judah under the figure of a woman who has gone whoring after foreign alliances and foreign gods, journeying to distant kings laden with costly ointments and perfumes meant to secure political favor rather than trusting the LORD who had covenanted with her. Debase names the trajectory of the whole transaction with brutal honesty: every costly gift sent abroad, every alliance purchased with perfume and flattery, is not advancement but descent, a self-lowering so complete the text says it reaches even unto hell. The irony is total, Judah believed these foreign courtships were the path to security and standing among the nations, while Isaiah insists the same actions were a debasement, trading covenant dignity as the LORD's own bride for the status of a client state begging survival from idols and their kings. Scripture's pattern here recurs whenever covenant people seek their security in something other than the LORD, status purchased this way is never actually gained, because the purchasing itself is the debasement, a people made lower precisely by what they imagined would make them safer.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from BASE: to reduce from a higher to a lower state; to degrade; to lower in value or dignity.
webster_full: BASE, a. Low in place, value, or dignity; without honor.
DEBASE, v.t. To reduce from a higher state; to degrade; to lower in dignity.
Isaiah 57: Judah debased herself by seeking security in foreign alliances rather than the LORD.
Describes a self-lowering that reaches, in Isaiah's own words, even unto hell.
Names the irony of seeking status by means that are themselves the debasement.
scriptures: Isa 57:9
And thou wentest to the king with ointment, and didst increase thy perfumes, and didst send thy messengers far off, and didst debase thyself even unto hell.
corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is that security purchased apart from the LORD is itself a debasement, however it is marketed as advancement.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Debase remains in common use with its sense largely intact, though mostly applied now to currency rather than covenant dignity.

Isaiah's indictment still names a live temptation: a believer or a church seeking standing and security through alliances, compromises, or courtships the world would recognize as savvy, while what is actually happening is the very debasement Isaiah describes. The path that looks like ascent, more influence, more favor, more perfume sent abroad, can be, by Scripture's own measure, a descent dressed as advancement.

roots_lines: Bassus, Latin for low, underlies base.

pos: v.t. (to announce formally as a threat or judgment; to proclaim as doomed)
etymology: From Old French denoncier, from Latin denuntiare, to announce formally, de- + nuntiare, to report; the KJV sense is an official declaration, not yet the accusatory sense of modern speech.
biblical_def:
I denounce unto you this day, that ye shall surely perish, and that ye shall not prolong your days upon the land, whither thou passest over Jordan to go to possess it.

Moses is closing his final charge to Israel with the covenant's own built-in warning, set alongside its promise in the same breath, I have set before you this day a blessing and a curse. Denounce here carries its older, formal sense, a solemn, official pronouncement rather than mere personal accusation, Moses speaking as covenant mediator to declare exactly what disobedience will cost before Israel has crossed a single step into the land. The verse's placement is deliberate, immediately after the famous call to choose life, that thou and thy seed may live, the denunciation names the real alternative being rejected, not a hypothetical but a specified, formally proclaimed consequence attached to apostasy and idol-worship. What makes this a denunciation rather than a prediction is its covenantal authority, Moses is not guessing at outcomes but declaring the terms both parties, the LORD and Israel, have already ratified; the warning's force comes entirely from the covenant it enforces, not from Moses's own rhetorical severity.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DENOUNCE: to proclaim in a formal or official manner, especially a threat, calamity, or evil to come.
webster_full: DENOUNCE, v.t. To proclaim, usually with threats; to declare officially as about to come.
DENOUNCEMENT, n. A formal proclamation of evil or judgment to come.
Deuteronomy 30: Moses formally denounces the covenant curse for disobedience.
Set directly alongside the covenant blessing in the same charge.
An official pronouncement under covenant authority, not a personal accusation.
scriptures: I denounce unto you this day, that ye shall surely perish, and that ye shall not prolong your days upon the land, whither thou passest over Jordan to go to possess it.
corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches, though the word's sense has narrowed considerably since the KJV's formal, covenantal usage.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Denounce has simply narrowed in modern speech to personal or political accusation, losing the KJV's older sense of a formal, authorized proclamation of covenant consequence.

The principle behind Moses's denunciation is still worth recovering: a true warning of judgment carries its weight not from the speaker's passion but from the authority behind it. Moses denounces nothing he has not already been given to proclaim; the church's own warnings of judgment likewise carry weight only so far as they are covenant-grounded declarations of what God has said, not personal severity dressed up as prophecy.

pos: v.t. (to abhor utterly; to hate as abominable)
etymology: From Latin detestari, to call heaven to witness against, de- + testari, to testify; the oldest sense is almost legal, swearing a formal witness of abhorrence.
biblical_def:
Neither shalt thou bring an abomination into thine house, lest thou be a cursed thing like it: but thou shalt utterly detest it, and thou shalt utterly abhor it; for it is a cursed thing.

Moses is commanding Israel's response to the carved images of the nations' gods, and the instruction is notably physical before it is emotional, thou shalt utterly detest it, and thou shalt utterly abhor it, a doubled command naming both a settled inward hatred and its necessary outward refusal. The warning behind the command is striking, lest thou be a cursed thing like it, as though proximity to an accursed object, bringing it even into one's own house, risks a kind of contagion, the curse transferring to whoever shelters what the LORD has already condemned. Detest here is not mere personal distaste; it is the only response compatible with covenant loyalty to a jealous God who has already pronounced sentence on these objects. The doubled utterly on both detest and abhor refuses half-measures, Israel is not permitted a curious tolerance or a decorative appreciation of what the LORD has cursed; the command asks for the same totality of rejection that the object's own cursedness already carries.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DETEST: to hate extremely; to abhor; to dislike utterly as abominable.
webster_full: DETEST, v.t. To hate extremely; to abhor; to abominate.
DETESTATION, n. Extreme hatred; abhorrence.
Deuteronomy 7: Israel must utterly detest and abhor the carved images of the nations.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Detest remains in ordinary use with its meaning largely intact, though applied to milder things than Moses's carved idols.

The command's logic still convicts a believer tempted to bring the accursed into the house, not literal idols now but the ideologies, entertainments, or practices Scripture has already named abominable, under the guise of merely studying or appreciating them. Moses's warning stands: bringing such a thing under one's own roof, even out of curiosity, risks becoming, in some measure, a cursed thing like it.

pos: adv. (clearly; openly; in a manner evident to all)
etymology: From manifest, Latin manifestus, caught in the hand, manus, hand, + a root meaning struck or seized; what is manifest is evidence so plain it is as if held in the hand.
biblical_def:
Forasmuch as ye are manifestly declared to be the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart.

Paul is defending his apostleship to a Corinthian church tempted to demand written credentials, and his answer inverts the whole category: the Corinthians themselves, their changed lives, are manifestly, visibly and beyond dispute, the only letter of recommendation Paul's ministry needs. Manifestly carries real weight here, Paul is not claiming a private conviction about the Corinthians' conversion but an evidence open to anyone's inspection, a transformation as plain as anything written in ink could be, except written instead by the Spirit of the living God on fleshy tables of the heart rather than stone. The deliberate echo of Moses's stone tablets sets up Paul's larger argument across the chapter, that the new covenant ministry he serves exceeds the old precisely in this, the law written on stone could command but not change the heart it addressed, while the Spirit's writing produces exactly the manifest, visible change Paul points to as his only certificate. The epistle of Christ that is manifestly read by all men is not a document at all but a life, which is Paul's whole point against those who wanted something smaller and more portable than a transformed church to examine.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from MANIFEST: evidently; clearly; in a manner open to the perception of all.
webster_full: MANIFEST, a. Evident to the senses; apparent; obvious.
MANIFESTLY, adv. Evidently; clearly; openly.
2 Corinthians 3: the Corinthians are manifestly declared to be the epistle of Christ.
Contrasted with the law written on stone, versus the Spirit's writing on the heart.
Names a visible, inspectable evidence, not merely a private conviction.

corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is that genuine ministry's only true credential is a manifestly changed life, not credentials on paper.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Manifestly remains in use with its meaning intact, clearly and openly, though it has become a somewhat formal word in ordinary speech.

Paul's argument still rebukes a church culture preoccupied with platforms, credentials, and polished presentation as proof of a ministry's legitimacy. The apostle's own defense was not a resume but manifestly changed lives, and any ministry today still has only that same certificate available to it, a people whose transformation by the Spirit is plain enough to be read by anyone, with or without paper credentials attached.

pos: adj./n. (regular; customary; the usual and settled provision)
etymology: From Latin ordinarius, regular, following order, from ordo, order; what is ordinary follows the fixed, settled pattern rather than the exceptional.
biblical_def:
Behold, therefore I have stretched out my hand over thee, and have diminished thine ordinary food, and delivered thee unto the will of them that hate thee, the daughters of the Philistines, which are ashamed of thy lewd way.

Ezekiel's indictment of Jerusalem under the figure of an unfaithful bride reaches a specific, almost domestic judgment here, the LORD diminishing her ordinary food, the settled, regular provision a covenant people had come to take for granted as simply how things were. The word measures the severity of the coming siege precisely by what it removes, not luxury but the ordinary, the baseline sustenance whose steady presence had let Jerusalem forget it was ever a gift rather than a given. There is a long biblical pattern behind this single verse, that the LORD's ordinary provision, daily bread, common grace, the unremarkable steadiness of rain and harvest, is itself a mercy easily mistaken for mere nature once its Giver is forgotten, and that covenant discipline often begins exactly where entitlement had settled in deepest, the merely ordinary. Ezekiel's Jerusalem is shamed even by the daughters of the Philistines, pagan onlookers scandalized by conduct that should have embarrassed the LORD's own covenant people first; diminished ordinary food becomes the visible sign of an invisible withdrawal that the city's own lewd way had already invited.

webster_full: ORDER, n. Regular arrangement; a settled method or course.
ORDINARY, a. According to established order; customary; usual.
Ezekiel 16: the LORD diminishes Jerusalem's ordinary food as covenant judgment.
Measures the coming siege's severity by the removal of settled, baseline provision.

scriptures: Behold, therefore I have stretched out my hand over thee, and have diminished thine ordinary food, and delivered thee unto the will of them that hate thee, the daughters of the Philistines, which are ashamed of thy lewd way.
corruption_summary: A spiritual culture hungry for the extraordinary has learned to despise the ordinary means of grace Ezekiel's word, read rightly, teaches a people to treasure.
corruption_paragraphs: Much contemporary spirituality prizes the extraordinary, dramatic encounters, visible signs, peak experiences, over the ordinary and steady, daily prayer, the regular preaching of the word, the settled rhythm of worship, treating the latter as spiritually thin precisely because it is ordinary.

Ezekiel's verse corrects the instinct from the opposite direction: the ordinary is exactly what covenant discipline removes to get a people's attention, which means the ordinary was never merely ordinary, it was mercy so constant it had stopped looking like mercy at all. A believer who despises the ordinary means of grace while chasing the extraordinary has mistaken the very thing Ezekiel's Jerusalem only learned to value after losing it.

pos: adj. (archaic spelling of public; open to common knowledge or view)
etymology: From Latin publicus, pertaining to the people, from populus, people; the KJV's older spelling, publick, is simply public before the final -k dropped from common English usage.
biblical_def:
Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily.

Matthew is narrating Joseph's private crisis before the angel's reassurance arrives, Mary found with child, and Joseph, under the law, holding real legal grounds to expose her, make her a publick example, a formal, shaming accusation with real legal consequence under Deuteronomy's provisions. The text calls Joseph a just man precisely in choosing not to pursue this public route even while he still believed, before the angel's explanation, that Mary had been unfaithful; his justice did not require public vindication of his own honor at the cost of her exposure. Publick example names the opposite of what Joseph chose, privily, a quiet, private resolution that would have spared Mary public shame without requiring Joseph to pretend no wrong had occurred. The word's placement is theologically significant, the Incarnation itself nearly began under the shadow of a public scandal that a just but still unenlightened man chose to avoid inflicting, before the angel's word transformed Joseph's private mercy into something he could not have anticipated, obedience to the actual purpose of God being worked out through the very situation he had resolved to handle so gently.

webster_full: PUBLIC, a. Open to common view or knowledge; pertaining to the people in general.
PUBLICK is the KJV's older spelling of the same word.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Publick is simply an archaic spelling; the word public carries the identical sense in modern English without alteration.

Joseph's restraint still corrects an age that treats public exposure as the default, even the righteous, response to a perceived wrong. A just man, Matthew says, chose privily over publick even while he still believed himself wronged, a restraint that made room for mercy, and, as it turned out, for the angel's correction, that a public response pursued first would have foreclosed.

pos: v.t. (to lay on as a burden, tax, or obligation; to require by authority)
etymology: From Latin imponere, to place upon, in- + ponere, to place; to set a weight or requirement upon something or someone.
biblical_def:
Also we certify you, that touching any of the priests and Levites, singers, porters, Nethinims, or ministers of this house of God, it shall not be lawful to impose toll, tribute, or custom, upon them.

This is part of King Artaxerxes's own decree, quoted at length in Ezra, granting the returned exiles not merely permission to rebuild but specific financial protections for those who serve the temple. A pagan king here forbids his own officials to impose toll, tribute, or custom on priests, Levites, singers, porters, and temple servants, a remarkable exemption from a Persian ruler who elsewhere in the same decree gives generously toward the temple's own worship out of royal treasury. The decree's logic, stated plainly a few verses later, is theological rather than merely diplomatic, why should damage grow to the hurt of the kings, a fear that the house of the God of heaven might be provoked to wrath against the realm itself if its ministers are burdened. Impose here names exactly what Artaxerxes forbids others to do and exactly what he himself does instead through generous provision, a contrast Ezra preserves carefully: the LORD's house received protection from imposed burdens precisely during a period when His people had no political power of their own to secure it, the LORD stirring even a foreign king's own self-interest into an instrument of covenant mercy.

webster_full: IMPOSE, v.t. To lay on; to set or place upon as a burden or charge.
IMPOSITION, n. The act of laying on a burden, tax, or requirement.
Ezra 7: Artaxerxes forbids his officials to impose toll, tribute, or custom on temple servants.
Part of a royal decree granting both protection and generous provision.
An instance of a pagan king's self-interest becoming an instrument of covenant mercy.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Impose remains in ordinary use with its sense intact, to lay a burden or requirement upon.

Ezra's narrative still rewards careful attention against any theology that expects the LORD's providence to work only through visibly righteous or sympathetic rulers. Artaxerxes forbids this imposition partly from genuine respect and partly from fear of provoking the God of heaven's wrath against his own realm; Scripture does not require his motive to be pure for the protection to be a real mercy to the LORD's people.

etymology: From injure, Latin injuria, a wrong, in-, not, + jus, right or law; to be injured is to be treated contrary to what is just.
biblical_def:
Brethren, I beseech you, be as I am; for I am as ye are: ye have not injured me at all.

Paul writes this in the middle of an unusually personal, almost wounded appeal to the Galatians, a church he planted that had since drifted toward a false gospel of circumcision and law-keeping pressed on them by other teachers. Ye have not injured me at all is Paul's deliberate reassurance before he presses his sharpest correction, clarifying that his coming confrontation is not personal grievance but pastoral alarm, he is not nursing a wound of his own but genuinely astonished, I marvel that ye are so soon removed, at their theological defection. The verse matters because it distinguishes two things an undiscerning reader might conflate, a teacher's hurt feelings and a teacher's legitimate doctrinal concern; Paul explicitly removes the first so the Galatians cannot dismiss his coming rebuke as merely wounded pride seeking vindication. Earlier in the same passage Paul recalls receiving them as an angel of God, even as Christ Jesus, despite his own physical infirmity, which makes injured carry real weight, he had every occasion for personal grievance and disclaims it anyway, so that what follows can be read for what it actually is, concern for their souls rather than concern for his own standing.

webster_full: INJURE, v.t. To do harm to; to wrong; to damage unjustly.
INJURED, a. Wronged; having suffered unjust harm or damage.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Injured remains in common use with the same sense, wronged or harmed, unaltered by modern reinterpretation.

Paul's disclaimer is a useful model against a tendency, ancient and modern alike, to let wounded personal pride masquerade as righteous doctrinal concern. He removes any suspicion of grievance before he corrects, so that the Galatians, and every later reader, can see the correction for what it actually is, concern for the gospel they were abandoning, not for an apostle's bruised feelings.

pos: n. (the skins of sheep, worn as rough garments; a mark of poverty or persecution)
etymology: From sheep, Old English sceap, + skin; the plainest possible garment, the hide of the flock rather than woven cloth.
biblical_def:
They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented.

The author of Hebrews is closing the great roll call of chapter eleven's faithful with a deliberate turn from triumph to suffering, having just listed those who escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, now naming those for whom faith produced not deliverance but destitution. Sheepskins and goatskins mark these saints as men and women reduced to the rudest covering available, the clothing of shepherds and the very poor, often while hiding from persecution in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth. The text refuses to treat this suffering as evidence of lesser faith than the triumphant list just before it; both groups belong to the same chapter, the same hall of faith, which of whom the world was not worthy. The verse corrects any theology that measures faith by visible outcome, these men and women in sheepskins possessed exactly the same faith that elsewhere stopped the mouths of lions and quenched the violence of fire, yet for them faith's reward was delayed entirely into the better resurrection the chapter has already named, not because their faith was smaller but because God had provided some better thing for us, that they without us should not be made perfect.

webster_full: SHEEPSKIN, n. The skin of a sheep, dressed with the wool on, worn as a garment.

The hall of faith's logic still corrects a prosperity-shaped theology that expects faith to reliably produce visible deliverance, strength, or comfort. Hebrews places the sheepskin-clad destitute in the identical chapter, under the identical faith, as those who escaped the edge of the sword, and insists both groups obtained a good report through faith, their differing outward fortunes notwithstanding.

pos: adj. (without mercy; showing no compassion toward the suffering or helpless)
etymology: From un-, negative, + merciful, from Latin merces, reward or pity; the negation of the quality that withholds deserved judgment out of compassion.
biblical_def:
Without understanding, covenantbreakers, without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful.

Paul closes his catalogue of Gentile depravity in Romans 1 with a list that descends from intellectual darkness to relational ruin, and unmerciful is its final, summary indictment, the last item in a sequence that begins with a mind given over to a reprobate mind and ends with the complete absence of compassion toward others. The word sits beside without natural affection and implacable deliberately, Paul is tracing how theological error, refusing to retain God in their knowledge, does not stay confined to doctrine but works itself out into the most basic structures of human relationship, even the affection a parent owes a child, even the mercy one creature owes another in need. Unmerciful names the terminus of this decline, a condition in which even the most minimal human compassion has been extinguished, not through a single catastrophic choice but as the settled outworking of having first exchanged the truth of God for a lie. Paul's larger argument in the chapter is that this entire catalogue, including its final unmerciful, is not merely bad behavior to be corrected by better manners but evidence of a mind under judgment, God gave them over, so that the only adequate remedy Paul will go on to describe is not moral improvement but the gospel itself.

corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is Paul's insistence that theological error eventually corrupts even the most basic human compassion.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Unmerciful remains in use with its sense intact, without mercy or compassion, unaltered by modern reinterpretation.

Paul's placement of the word still resists a common modern instinct to separate doctrine from character, as though what a society believes about God has no bearing on how it treats its weakest members. Romans 1 traces the opposite: a mind that has exchanged the truth of God for a lie does not stay merely wrong in its theology, it ends, by the chapter's own account, unmerciful, incapable even of the basic compassion owed to those who cannot repay it.
